Backup: the most important differing metrics decide

Let \(\mathcal{M}_{x,y}\) be the metrics on which \(x\) and \(y\) differ.
Then \(x \prec_{\mathcal{M},P} y\) if and only if \(\mathcal{M}_{x,y} \neq \emptyset\) and \(m(x) < m(y)\) for every maximal metric \(m\) of \(\mathcal{M}_{x,y}\).
\((\mathcal{M}, P)\)

\(m_1\)\(m_2\)\(m_3\)\(m_4\)
\(x\)0101
\(y\)1010

• \(x\) and \(y\) differ on every metric; the maximal ones are \(m_1\) and \(m_3\), and \(x\) is better on both
  • so \(x \prec y\): the losses on \(m_2\) and \(m_4\) lie below the gains

Backup: pre-orders on metrics and pre-ordered values

If \({\prec_P} \subseteq {\prec_{P'}}\), then \({\preceq_{\mathcal{M},P}} \subseteq {\preceq_{\mathcal{M},P'}}\).
Under the same condition, \(\operatorname{Min}(\mathcal{X}, \preceq_{\mathcal{M},P'}) \subseteq \operatorname{Min}(\mathcal{X}, \preceq_{\mathcal{M},P})\) as well.

• more strict pairs on the metrics give more comparisons of decisions, and a smaller optimal set
  • a pre-order \(P\) on the metrics induces the same order on \(\mathcal{X}\) as its strict part, so partial orders lose nothing
  • pre-ordered values: a loss is a value that is not at most the other one
  • for one metric with incomparable values \(m(x) = a\) and \(m(y) = b\):
    • the rule books of Censi et al. (2019) make \(x\) and \(y\) equivalent
    • here \(x\) and \(y\) are incomparable, as their values are
Backup: infinitely many metrics break the order
\((\mathcal{M}, P)\)

\(m_1\)\(m_2\)\(m_3\)\(m_4\)\(\cdots\)
\(x\)0000\(\cdots\)
\(y\)−11−11\(\cdots\)
\(z\)1000\(\cdots\)

• here \(m_{k+1}\) lies above \(m_k\), because the chain has no top
  • against \(y\), each loss of \(x\) has a gain on the next metric, and vice versa: \(x \sim y\), though they differ on every metric
  • \(z\) differs from \(x\) only on \(m_1\), and the same gains give \(y \sim z\)
  • so \(z \preceq y \preceq x\), yet \(z\) loses to \(x\) on \(m_1\) with no gain: transitivity fails
  • with finitely many metrics, \(\preceq_{\mathcal{M},P}\) is a pre-order and the maximal differing metrics decide

• \(x \preceq_{\mathcal{M},P} y\) if and only if \(x \preceq_{\mathcal{M},P'} y\) for every lexicographic extension \(P'\) of \(P\), a total order that contains \(P\)
  • here the extensions put \(m_1\) or \(m_2\) first, and their optimal sets are \(\{a\}\) and \(\{b\}\)
  • \(c\) is optimal for \(P\), with \(\mathcal{X}^* = \{a, b, c\}\), yet optimal for no lexicographic extension
  • the layered extension \((\{m_1, m_2\})\) keeps \(c\): layers, not lexicographic orders, cover \(\mathcal{X}^*\) for convex metrics

Backup: why convexity lets layered extensions reach every optimum

For each upper set \(U \neq \mathcal{M}\), let \(A = \operatorname{Max}(\mathcal{M} \setminus U)\).
Then \(y \prec_{\mathcal{M},P} x\) if and only if, for some such \(U\), \(y\) is no worse than \(x\) on \(U\) and better on every metric of \(A\).

The shielding order is a partial order.
The order that the shielding order induces on \(\mathcal{X}\) lies in \(\preceq_{\mathcal{C}}\).
The two orders are equal when every metric has a faithful chain.
A faithful chain of a metric \(m\) is a chain in which each metric above \(m\) lies above \(m\) in the shielding order.

• here \(C_1\) is faithful for \(m_1, m_3\) and \(C_2\) for \(m_2, m_4\), so the shielding order gives \(\preceq_{\mathcal{C}}\)
  • the union order merges the cycle of \(m_1, m_2, m_3\) and differs from \(\preceq_{\mathcal{C}}\)
Backup: the union order adds and misses comparisons
\(\mathcal{C} = (C_1, C_2)\)

\(m_1\)\(m_2\)\(m_3\)\(m_4\)
\(x\)0010

• \(x\) loses to \(y\) on \(m_3\) and gains on \(m_1\): \(C_1\) puts \(m_1\) above \(m_3\), and \(C_2\) holds no \(m_3\), so \(x \preceq_{\mathcal{C}} y\)
  • the union order puts nothing strictly above \(m_3\), so it misses \(x \preceq y\)
  • \(x'\) loses to \(y'\) on \(m_4\) and gains on \(m_3\): \(C_2\), the one chain with \(m_4\), holds no \(m_3\), so \(x' \not\preceq_{\mathcal{C}} y'\)
  • the union order puts \(m_3\) above \(m_4\), so it adds \(x' \preceq y'\)
  • the shielding order agrees with \(\preceq_{\mathcal{C}}\) on both pairs, as the theorem says

• \(\mathcal{X}\): the convex hull of the curve \(y_s = (1 + s,\ 1 - s + s^2,\ 1)\), \(s \in [0, 1/2]\), and the point \(c = (1, 1, 7/8)\)
  • the weights \(i^2,\ i^2 + i,\ 1\) represent \(P\), with the layers \((\{m_1, m_2\}, \{m_3\})\)
  • \(S_i(y_s) - S_i(y_0) = -i s + (i^2 + i) s^2\) is least at \(s = 1/(2(i+1))\), at most \(-1/6\) for \(i \geq 2\), below \(S_i(c) - S_i(y_0) = -1/8\)
  • \(S_i\) is linear, so \(x_i = y_{1/(2(i+1))}\) is its only minimum on \(\mathcal{X}\), and \(x_i \to x_0 = (1, 1, 1)\)
  • \(\textcolor{dpred}{c}\) agrees with \(\textcolor{dpred}{x_0}\) on \(\textcolor{dpred}{B_1}\) and is better on \(\textcolor{dpred}{m_3}\), so \(\textcolor{dpred}{x_0 \notin \mathcal{X}^*_P}\)
  • the curve trades \(m_1\) for \(m_2\) at the cost \(s^2\): leaving \(x_0\) along it gains about \(1/4\), more than the \(1/8\) of \(c\)
Backup: targeting families against minimal layered extensions

For metrics \(\max\{f_m, 0\}\) with \(f_m\) strictly convex, every family that targets every upper set gives \(\mathcal{X}^*_P\).
For convex metrics, only the minimal layered extensions are sure to give \(\mathcal{X}^*_P\).

• a targeting family is a smallest cover of the upper sets by chains of \(\sqsubseteq\), found by a matching
  • the minimal layered extensions merge every two consecutive layers that form an antichain
  • neither family is always the smaller, and a targeting family can miss a minimal layered extension
